Why most plantations fail

Four fixable reasons account for most sapling deaths. GreenPlan scores every plan against all four.

📍

Wrong place

No space for roots, no sunlight, or a site that floods. We check district, soil and site fit first.

🌳

Wrong species

Exotic or thirsty species in dry soil rarely survive. We match native species to your soil and water.

🗓️

Wrong timing

Planting in peak summer or deep winter starves roots. The monsoon window changes everything.

💧

No follow-up

A photo on planting day isn't care. Watering logs and health checks keep survival visible.

The Maharashtra monsoon window

Drag through the year — timing alone can swing survival by 30+ points.

Best: late June – July, when soil is moist and rain does the first watering for you. December planting needs a prep + irrigation plan — try it in the Planner and watch the score change.

Learn to grow, not just plant

Short, practical guides — plus a searchable species library with water, soil and size data.

1 · Choose the right species

Native species survive because they evolved with local rain, soil and pests. As a rule: dry districts (Nagpur, Sambhajinagar) favour Neem, Karanj and Tamarind; wetter districts (Kolhapur, Thane) support Jamun, Mango and Rain Tree. Avoid thirsty exotics where water is tanker-dependent — the Planner penalises exactly this mismatch.

  • Match canopy to space: a Banyan needs 15m+ — never plant it under wires or near foundations.
  • Mix species: a single-species row can lose everything to one pest. Aim for at least 3 species.
  • Fruit species (Jamun, Mango, Tamarind) bring birds, people and long-term protectors.
2 · Read your soil before you dig

Black cotton soil holds water well but cracks when dry — great for Neem, Tamarind, Jamun; mulch heavily. Red/laterite drains fast — Karanj and Bahava do well; add compost to the pit. Rocky/shallow soil needs drought-hardy species (Neem, Karanj) and a deeper 2×2×2 ft pit. Sandy soil needs frequent early watering and wind protection.

3 · Timing is half the battle

Late June to July is Maharashtra's golden window: soil is moist, humidity is high, and rain handles early watering. Winter planting (Nov–Feb) can work with assured irrigation and mulch, but growth pauses. Peak summer (Mar–May) planting without daily water is the single biggest cause of first-year death.

4 · Watering: the first 90 days decide everything
  • Weeks 1–2: water daily in dry weather (5–10 litres per sapling).
  • Weeks 3–8: every alternate day; check soil moisture a finger deep.
  • Months 3–12: twice a week in summer, once a week otherwise; deep watering beats sprinkling.
  • Always water early morning or evening — midday water mostly evaporates.
5 · Maintenance that actually happens

Mulch a 1-metre ring (dry leaves/compost) to hold moisture and block weeds. Add a tree guard where cattle or traffic threaten saplings. Assign a named caretaker or rota — “everyone's tree” quickly becomes no one's tree. Log health monthly; yellowing leaves + dry soil = water stress, yellowing + wet soil = root trouble.

6 · What's next: photo-based health AI (roadmap)

Our roadmap adds image-based health analysis: leaf-colour and canopy checks from a phone photo, early stress flags, disease-pattern alerts and personalised care recommendations. In this prototype, try the demo in Health Check — it shows the intended experience with a clearly-labelled demo model, not a live diagnosis.
